claim: The adult brain demonstrates remarkable multisensory plasticity by dynamically recalibrating itself based on information from multiple sensory sources.
source: The adult brain demonstrates remarkable multisensory plasticity by dynamically recalibrating itself based on information from multiple sensory sources.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: After a systematic visual–vestibular heading offset is experienced, the unisensory perceptual estimates for subsequently presented stimuli are shifted toward each other (in opposite directions) to reduce the conflict.
source: After a systematic visual–vestibular heading offset is experienced, the unisensory perceptual estimates for subsequently presented stimuli are shifted toward each other (in opposite directions) to reduce the conflict.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data presented in Figure 2, showing opposite shifts in vestibular and visual psychometric curves.

claim: Both visual and vestibular neuronal tuning curves in MSTd shifted – each according to their respective cues' perceptual shifts.
source: Both visual and vestibular neuronal tuning curves in MSTd shifted – each according to their respective cues' perceptual shifts.
evidence: This claim is supported by the neuronal data presented in Figure 3, showing correlations between neuronal and perceptual shifts in MSTd.

claim: Tuning of vestibular neurons in PIVC shifted in the same direction as vestibular perceptual shifts.
source: Tuning of vestibular neurons in PIVC also shifted in the same direction as vestibular perceptual shifts (cells were not robustly tuned to the visual stimuli).
evidence: This claim is supported by the neuronal data presented in Figure 4, showing positive correlation between vestibular neuronal and perceptual shifts in PIVC.

claim: PIVC cells were not robustly tuned to the visual stimuli.
source: Tuning of vestibular neurons in PIVC also shifted in the same direction as vestibular perceptual shifts (cells were not robustly tuned to the visual stimuli).
evidence: This claim is supported by the lack of significant visual tuning in PIVC neurons as shown in Figure 4.

claim: Both vestibular and visual tuning in VIP shifted in accordance with vestibular perceptual shifts.
source: By contrast, VIP neurons demonstrated a unique phenomenon: both vestibular and visual tuning shifted in accordance with vestibular perceptual shifts.
evidence: This claim is supported by the neuronal data presented in Figure 5, showing that both vestibular and visual neuronal shifts in VIP correlated with vestibular perceptual shifts.

claim: Visual tuning in VIP shifted contrary to visual perceptual shifts.
source: Such that, visual tuning shifted, surprisingly, contrary to visual perceptual shifts.
evidence: This claim is supported by the negative correlation between visual neuronal shifts and visual perceptual shifts in VIP shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Unsupervised recalibration (to reduce cue conflict) occurs in early multisensory cortices.
source: Therefore, while unsupervised recalibration (to reduce cue conflict) occurs in early multisensory cortices, higher-level VIP reflects only a global shift, in vestibular space.
evidence: This claim is supported by the findings in MSTd and PIVC showing modality-specific recalibration that matches perceptual shifts.

claim: Higher-level VIP reflects only a global shift, in vestibular space.
source: Therefore, while unsupervised recalibration (to reduce cue conflict) occurs in early multisensory cortices, higher-level VIP reflects only a global shift, in vestibular space.
evidence: This claim is supported by the finding that both visual and vestibular tuning in VIP shifted together in accordance with vestibular perceptual shifts.

claim: The neural substrate of visual-vestibular recalibration was unknown prior to this study.
source: The neural substrate of this recalibration is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge before the current study.

claim: Single-neuron activity was recorded from the dorsal medial superior temporal (MSTd), parietoinsular vestibular cortex (PIVC), and ventral intraparietal (VIP) areas in three male rhesus macaques during visual–vestibular recalibration.
source: Here, we recorded single-neuron activity from the dorsal medial superior temporal (MSTd), parietoinsular vestibular cortex (PIVC), and ventral intraparietal (VIP) areas in three male rhesus macaques during this visual–vestibular recalibration.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Different sensory systems each continuously adapt to changes in the environment.
source: Our different sensory systems each continuously adapt to changes in the environment (Webster, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Webster, 2012.

claim: The brain needs to dynamically adjust for sensory discrepancies between different modalities to maintain stable and coherent perception in a multisensory and ever-changing world.
source: Thus, to maintain stable and coherent perception in a multisensory and ever-changing world, the brain needs to dynamically adjust for sensory discrepancies between the different modalities.
evidence: This is a general statement about brain function that is supported by the broader context of the study.

claim: Multisensory recalibration takes place continually and is perhaps more fundamental than multisensory integration because integration would not be beneficial when the underlying cues are biased.
source: This process of multisensory recalibration takes place continually and is perhaps more fundamental than multisensory integration because integration would not be beneficial when the underlying cues are biased.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the relative importance of recalibration vs. integration.

claim: The neural bases of multisensory integration have received a lot of attention.
source: While the neural bases of multisensory integration have received a lot of attention (Chen et al., 2013a; Gu et al., 2008; Stein et al., 2014), the neural bases of multisensory recalibration have been explored to a much lesser degree.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2013a; Gu et al., 2008; Stein et al., 2014.

claim: The neural bases of multisensory recalibration have been explored to a much lesser degree than multisensory integration.
source: While the neural bases of multisensory integration have received a lot of attention (Chen et al., 2013a; Gu et al., 2008; Stein et al., 2014), the neural bases of multisensory recalibration have been explored to a much lesser degree.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field based on the literature.

claim: Cross-modal recalibration has been observed in a variety of multisensory settings.
source: Cross-modal recalibration has been observed in a variety of multisensory settings.
evidence: This claim is supported by the examples provided in the subsequent text.

claim: The ventriloquist aftereffect is an example of cross-modal recalibration in which exposure to a consistent spatial discrepancy between auditory and visual stimuli induces a subsequent shift in the perceived location of sounds.
source: One well-known example is the ventriloquist aftereffect, in which exposure to a consistent spatial discrepancy between auditory and visual stimuli induces a subsequent shift in the perceived location of sounds (Bertelson and De Gelder, 2004; Canon, 1970; Kramer et al., 2019; Radeau and Bertelson, 1974; Recanzone, 1998; Watson et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bertelson and De Gelder, 2004; Canon, 1970; Kramer et al., 2019; Radeau and Bertelson, 1974; Recanzone, 1998; Watson et al., 2021.

claim: The rubber-hand illusion leads to an offset in hand proprioception in the direction of the visually observed rubber hand.
source: Also, the rubber-hand illusion leads to an offset in hand proprioception in the direction of the visually observed rubber hand (Abdulkarim et al., 2021; Botvinick and Cohen, 1998; Kennett et al., 2001; Thériault et al., 2022; Tsakiris and Haggard, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Abdulkarim et al., 2021; Botvinick and Cohen, 1998; Kennett et al., 2001; Thériault et al., 2022; Tsakiris and Haggard, 2005.

claim: It was initially thought that only the non-visual cues recalibrate to vision, termed visual dominance.
source: Although it was initially thought that only the non-visual cues recalibrate to vision, termed visual dominance (Brainard and Knudsen, 1993; Rock and Victor, 1964), further work in a variety of paradigms has revealed both visual and non-visual recalibration (Atkins et al., 2003; Lewald, 2002; van Beers et al., 2002; Zaidel et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brainard and Knudsen, 1993; Rock and Victor, 1964.

claim: Further work in a variety of paradigms has revealed both visual and non-visual recalibration.
source: Although it was initially thought that only the non-visual cues recalibrate to vision, termed visual dominance (Brainard and Knudsen, 1993; Rock and Victor, 1964), further work in a variety of paradigms has revealed both visual and non-visual recalibration (Atkins et al., 2003; Lewald, 2002; van Beers et al., 2002; Zaidel et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Atkins et al., 2003; Lewald, 2002; van Beers et al., 2002; Zaidel et al., 2011.

claim: Most of what we know about multisensory recalibration is described at the behavioral level, with little known about its neuronal underpinnings.
source: Most of what we know about multisensory recalibration is described at the behavioral level (Lewald, 2002), with little known about its neuronal underpinnings.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: In the ventriloquism aftereffect, cross-modal (audio-visual) recalibration of auditory signals (fMRI) is seen in low-level auditory cortical areas.
source: In the ventriloquism aftereffect, cross-modal (audio-visual) recalibration of auditory signals (fMRI) is seen in low-level auditory cortical areas (Zierul et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zierul et al., 2017.

claim: Higher-level parietal regions play a central role in cross-modal spatial recalibration.
source: According to that study and another recent (EEG) study (Park and Kayser, 2021), higher-level parietal regions also play a central role in cross-modal spatial recalibration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies by Zierul et al., 2017 and Park and Kayser, 2021.

claim: Frontal regions consolidate the behavioral shift under sustained multisensory discrepancies.
source: Moreover, Park and Kayser, 2021 further suggest that frontal regions consolidate the behavioral shift under sustained multisensory discrepancies.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Park and Kayser, 2021.

claim: fMRI and EEG methods lack the resolution to probe recalibration at the level of single neurons.
source: However, these methods (fMRI and EEG) lack the resolution to probe recalibration at the level of single neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of fMRI and EEG methods.

claim: Knudsen and Brainard investigated multisensory plasticity at the neuronal and circuit levels in the barn owl.
source: In a series of classic studies, Kundsen and Brainard investigated multisensory plasticity at the neuronal and circuit levels in the barn owl (Knudsen, 2002; Knudsen and Brainard, 1991; Linkenhoker and Knudsen, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Knudsen, 2002; Knudsen and Brainard, 1991; Linkenhoker and Knudsen, 2002.

claim: Profound neuronal plasticity was found in juvenile owls reared with prismatic lenses that systematically displaced their field of view.
source: They found profound neuronal plasticity in juvenile owls reared with prismatic lenses that systematically displaced their field of view.
evidence: This claim is supported by the citations to Knudsen and Brainard's work.

claim: The auditory space map in the optic tectum of juvenile owls was recalibrated to be aligned with the displaced visual field.
source: In that case, the auditory space map in the optic tectum was recalibrated to be aligned with the displaced visual field (Knudsen and Brainard, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Knudsen and Brainard, 1991.

claim: Multisensory plasticity is not limited to development.
source: However, multisensory plasticity is not limited to the development, and the neuronal bases of how multiple sensory systems continuously adapt to one another in the adult brain remain fundamentally unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the scope of multisensory plasticity.

claim: The neuronal bases of how multiple sensory systems continuously adapt to one another in the adult brain remain fundamentally unknown.
source: However, multisensory plasticity is not limited to the development, and the neuronal bases of how multiple sensory systems continuously adapt to one another in the adult brain remain fundamentally unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Self-motion perception relies primarily on visual and vestibular cues.
source: Self-motion perception (the subjective feeling of moving through space) relies primarily on visual and vestibular cues (Butler et al., 2015; Butler et al., 2010; de Winkel et al., 2010; Fetsch et al., 2011; Fetsch et al., 2009; Gu et al., 2007; Warren et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Butler et al., 2015; Butler et al., 2010; de Winkel et al., 2010; Fetsch et al., 2011; Fetsch et al., 2009; Gu et al., 2007; Warren et al., 1988.

claim: Multisensory integration of visual and vestibular signals can improve heading perception.
source: Multisensory integration of visual and vestibular signals can improve heading perception (Butler et al., 2015; Dokka et al., 2015; Gu et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Butler et al., 2015; Dokka et al., 2015; Gu et al., 2008.

claim: Conflicting or inconsistent visual and vestibular information often leads to motion sickness.
source: However, conflicting or inconsistent visual and vestibular information often leads to motion sickness (Oman, 1990; Reason and Brand, 1975).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Oman, 1990; Reason and Brand, 1975.

claim: Motion sickness subsides after prolonged exposure to sensory motion conflict, presumably through brain mechanisms of multisensory recalibration.
source: Interestingly, this subsides after prolonged exposure to the sensory motion conflict, presumably through brain mechanisms of multisensory recalibration (Held, 1961; Shupak and Gordon, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Held, 1961; Shupak and Gordon, 2006.

claim: Robust perceptual recalibration of both visual and vestibular cues was found in response to a systematic vestibular–visual heading discrepancy.
source: We previously investigated and found robust perceptual recalibration of both visual and vestibular cues in response to a systematic vestibular–visual heading discrepancy (Zaidel et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zaidel et al., 2011.

claim: Similar perceptual recalibration results were seen for both humans and monkeys.
source: Similar results were seen for both humans and monkeys.
evidence: This refers to the results from Zaidel et al., 2011.

claim: In the unsupervised recalibration paradigm, no external feedback was given.
source: In that paradigm, no external feedback was given.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental paradigm used in Zaidel et al., 2011.

claim: The need for recalibration arose solely because of the cue discrepancy in the unsupervised condition.
source: Thus, the need for recalibration arose solely because of the cue discrepancy (we therefore call this condition unsupervised).
evidence: This is a description of the unsupervised recalibration paradigm.

claim: Unsupervised recalibration led to shifts in subsequent visual and vestibular perceptual estimates toward each other, presumably to reduce the conflict.
source: This led to shifts in subsequent visual and vestibular perceptual estimates toward each other, presumably to reduce the conflict.
evidence: This is a description of the results from Zaidel et al., 2011.

claim: Unsupervised recalibration aims to maintain 'internal consistency' between the cues.
source: This is in line with the notion that unsupervised recalibration aims to maintain 'internal consistency' between the cues (Burge et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Burge et al., 2010.

claim: The neuronal basis of visual-vestibular recalibration was unknown prior to this study.
source: However, the neuronal basis of this everyday multisensory plasticity is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge before the current study.

claim: Human neuroimaging studies showed cross-modal (auditory–visual) recalibration in relatively early sensory areas.
source: In line with human neuroimaging studies that showed cross-modal (auditory–visual) recalibration in relatively early sensory areas (Amedi et al., 2002; Zierul et al., 2017), and because unsupervised recalibration is sensory driven (occurs as a result of the cross-modal discrepancy, in the absence of overt feedback) we expected to observe neural correlates of unsupervised visual–vestibular recalibration in relatively early cortical areas with self-motion signals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Amedi et al., 2002; Zierul et al., 2017.

claim: Unsupervised recalibration is sensory driven (occurs as a result of the cross-modal discrepancy, in the absence of overt feedback).
source: In line with human neuroimaging studies that showed cross-modal (auditory–visual) recalibration in relatively early sensory areas (Amedi et al., 2002; Zierul et al., 2017), and because unsupervised recalibration is sensory driven (occurs as a result of the cross-modal discrepancy, in the absence of overt feedback) we expected to observe neural correlates of unsupervised visual–vestibular recalibration in relatively early cortical areas with self-motion signals.
evidence: This is a characterization of unsupervised recalibration based on the experimental design.

claim: MSTd and PIVC are two relatively early multisensory cortical areas involved in self-motion perception.
source: Previous studies with monkeys identified two relatively early multisensory cortical areas involved in self-motion perception: the medial superior temporal area (Gu et al., 2006) and the parietal insular vestibular cortex (PIVC, Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gu et al., 2006 and Chen et al., 2010.

claim: Neurons in MSTd respond to large optic flow stimuli, conducive to the visual perception of self-motion.
source: Neurons in MSTd respond to large optic flow stimuli, conducive to the visual perception of self-motion (Gu et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gu et al., 2006.

claim: Vestibular responses are present in MSTd, however visual self-motion signals dominate.
source: Vestibular responses are also present in MSTd, however visual self-motion signals dominate (Gu, 2018; Gu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gu, 2018; Gu et al., 2012.

claim: PIVC has strong vestibular responses, without strong tuning to visual optic flow.
source: PIVC has strong vestibular responses, without strong tuning to visual optic flow (Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2010.

claim: VIP has robust responses to visual and vestibular self-motion stimuli.
source: The ventral intraparietal (VIP) area also has robust responses to visual and vestibular self-motion stimuli, however, it is marked by strong choice signals (Chen et al., 2016; Gu, 2018; Zaidel et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2016; Gu, 2018; Zaidel et al., 2017.

claim: VIP is marked by strong choice signals.
source: The ventral intraparietal (VIP) area also has robust responses to visual and vestibular self-motion stimuli, however, it is marked by strong choice signals (Chen et al., 2016; Gu, 2018; Zaidel et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2016; Gu, 2018; Zaidel et al., 2017.

claim: VIP is considered a higher-level multisensory area, possibly involved in perceptual decision-making or higher-order perceptual functions.
source: It is thus considered a higher-level multisensory area, possibly involved in perceptual decision-making or higher-order perceptual functions.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the properties of VIP neurons.

claim: Parietal regions are involved in human cross-modal recalibration.
source: Accordingly, and in line with findings of parietal involvement in human cross-modal recalibration (Park and Kayser, 2021; Zaidel et al., 2021; Zierul et al., 2017), we were interested to see what correlates of unsupervised recalibration we would see in parietal neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Park and Kayser, 2021; Zaidel et al., 2021; Zierul et al., 2017.

claim: Three monkeys performed a heading discrimination task before, during, and after undergoing cross-modal recalibration to spatially conflicting vestibular–visual signals.
source: Three monkeys performed a heading discrimination task before, during, and after undergoing cross-modal recalibration to spatially conflicting vestibular–visual signals.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Single neurons were recorded extracellularly in areas MSTd (N = 83 total; 19 from monkey D, 64 from monkey K), PIVC (N = 160 total; 91 from monkey D, 69 from monkey B), and VIP (N = 118 total; 103 from monkey D, 15 from monkey B).
source: Simultaneous to behavioral performance, we recorded from single neurons extracellularly in areas MSTd (upper bank of the superior temporal sulcus, N = 83 total; 19 from monkey D, 64 from monkey K), PIVC (upper bank and the tip of the lateral sulcus, N = 160 total; 91 from monkey D, 69 from monkey B), and VIP (lower bank and tip of the intraparietal sulcus, N = 118 total; 103 from monkey D, 15 from monkey B).
evidence: This is a description of the data collection.

claim: The experiment paradigm consisted of three consecutive blocks: pre-recalibration, recalibration, and post-recalibration.
source: It consisted of three consecutive blocks: pre-recalibration (Figure 1A), recalibration (Figure 1B), and post-recalibration (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design shown in Figure 1.

claim: In the recalibration block, the monkeys were presented with combined stimuli (simultaneous visual and vestibular cues) with a systematic discrepancy between the visual and vestibular heading directions.
source: In the recalibration block, the monkeys were presented with combined stimuli (simultaneous visual and vestibular cues) with a systematic discrepancy between the visual and vestibular heading directions.
evidence: This is a description of the recalibration block procedure.

claim: In the pre- and post-recalibration blocks, the unisensory perception was measured using visual-only or vestibular-only cues.
source: In the pre- and post-recalibration blocks, the unisensory perception was measured using visual-only or vestibular-only cues.
evidence: This is a description of the pre- and post-recalibration block procedures.

claim: The effects of recalibration on visual and vestibular perception were measured by the shifts in the post- vs. pre-recalibration psychometric curves.
source: The effects of recalibration on visual and vestibular perception were measured by the shifts in the post- vs. pre-recalibration psychometric curves.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method.

claim: Both visual and vestibular psychometric functions shifted in the direction required to reduce cue conflict.
source: Replicating our previous behavioral results (Zaidel et al., 2011), we found that both visual and vestibular psychometric functions shifted in the direction required to reduce cue conflict.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: When the vestibular and visual heading stimuli were systematically offset such that they consistently deviated to the right and the left, respectively (Δ+), the vestibular post-recalibration curve was shifted rightward vs. pre-recalibration.
source: Namely, when the vestibular and visual heading stimuli were systematically offset, such that they consistently deviated to the right and the left, respectively (Δ+, Figure 2A), the vestibular post-recalibration curve (blue) was shifted rightward vs. pre-recalibration (black).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A rightward shift of the psychometric curve indicates a leftward perceptual shift.
source: Note that a rightward shift of the psychometric curve indicates a leftward perceptual shift (identified by a lower propensity for 'rightward' choices at 0° heading for the blue curve).
evidence: This is an explanation of how to interpret psychometric curve shifts.

claim: The visual post-recalibration psychometric curve shifted leftward vs. pre-recalibration, albeit to a lesser degree, indicating a rightward perceptual shift.
source: Complementarily, the visual post-recalibration psychometric curve (red) shifted leftward vs. pre-recalibration (black), albeit to a lesser degree, indicating a rightward perceptual shift.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: When the vestibular and visual heading stimuli were offset to the left and right, respectively (Δ−), the vestibular post-recalibration curve shifted to the left, and the visual post-recalibration curve shifted to the right.
source: In a reverse manner, when the vestibular and visual heading stimuli were offset to the left and right, respectively (Δ−, Figure 2B), the vestibular post-recalibration curve (blue) shifted to the left, and the visual post-recalibration curve shifted to the right.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In each session, only one discrepancy orientation was tested.
source: In each session, only one discrepancy orientation was tested.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Data were collected from 241 sessions with Δ+ and 227 sessions with Δ−.
source: In total, we collected data from 241 sessions with Δ+ and 227 sessions with Δ−.
evidence: This is a description of the dataset.

claim: The vestibular PSEs were shifted significantly to the right for the Δ+ condition (mean ± SE = 1.12° ± 0.12°; p = 2.3 × 10−17, paired t-test).
source: The vestibular PSEs were shifted significantly to the right for the Δ+ condition (mean ± SE = 1.12° ± 0.12°; p = 2.3 × 10−17, paired t-test), and significantly to the left for the Δ− condition (mean ± SE = −1.76° ± 0.14°; p = 1.0 × 10−28, paired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The vestibular PSEs were shifted significantly to the left for the Δ− condition (mean ± SE = −1.76° ± 0.14°; p = 1.0 × 10−28, paired t-test).
source: The vestibular PSEs were shifted significantly to the right for the Δ+ condition (mean ± SE = 1.12° ± 0.12°; p = 2.3 × 10−17, paired t-test), and significantly to the left for the Δ− condition (mean ± SE = −1.76° ± 0.14°; p = 1.0 × 10−28, paired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The visual PSEs were shifted significantly to the left for the Δ+ condition (mean ± SE = −0.73° ± 0.11°; p = 6.5 × 10−11, paired t-test).
source: The visual PSEs were shifted significantly to the left for the Δ+ condition (mean ± SE = −0.73° ± 0.11°; p = 6.5 × 10−11, paired t-test), and significantly to the right for the Δ− condition (mean ± SE = 1.10° ± 0.10°; p = 5.4 × 10−23, paired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The visual PSEs were shifted significantly to the right for the Δ− condition (mean ± SE = 1.10° ± 0.10°; p = 5.4 × 10−23, paired t-test).
source: The visual PSEs were shifted significantly to the left for the Δ+ condition (mean ± SE = −0.73° ± 0.11°; p = 6.5 × 10−11, paired t-test), and significantly to the right for the Δ− condition (mean ± SE = 1.10° ± 0.10°; p = 5.4 × 10−23, paired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Both cues shifted (in opposite directions) to reduce cue conflict.
source: Thus, consistent with our previous study, both cues shifted (in opposite directions) to reduce cue conflict.
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Vestibular shifts were significantly larger than visual shifts (1.43° ± 0.09° and 0.91° ± 0.07°, respectively; p = 6.8 × 10−5, paired t-test).
source: Comparing the vestibular vs. visual shift magnitudes (pooled by flipping the vestibular and visual shift signs in the Δ− and Δ+ conditions, respectively) demonstrated significantly larger vestibular vs. visual shifts (1.43° ± 0.09° and 0.91° ± 0.07°, respectively; p = 6.8 × 10−5, paired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The behavioral results from the original study (performed in the Angelaki laboratory) were replicated in these experiments (in the Chen laboratory) using a new set of monkeys, with simultaneous neuronal recording.
source: Thus, the behavioral results from the original study (performed in the Angelaki laboratory) were replicated in these experiments (in the Chen laboratory) using a new set of monkeys, with simultaneous neuronal recording.
evidence: This is a statement about the replication of previous findings.

claim: For an example MSTd neuron, the vestibular neurometric curve shifted to the right, while the visual neurometric curve shifted to the left.
source: For this MSTd neuron, the vestibular neurometric curve shifted to the right, while the visual neurometric curve shifted to the left.
evidence: This claim is supported by the example shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The shifts in vestibular and visual tuning in the example MSTd neuron were consistent with the perceptual shifts.
source: Thus, the shifts in vestibular and visual tuning were consistent with the perceptual shifts.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the example shown in Figure 3A.

claim: MSTd neuronal shifts were significantly correlated with the perceptual shifts, both for vestibular and visual cues (r = 0.62, p = 0.019, N = 14, and r = 0.38, p = 2.7 × 10−3, N = 59, respectively; Pearson correlations, data pooled across monkeys).
source: The MSTd neuronal shifts were significantly correlated with the perceptual shifts, both for vestibular and visual cues (r = 0.62, p = 0.019, N = 14, and r = 0.38, p = 2.7 × 10−3, N = 59, respectively; Pearson correlations, data pooled across monkeys).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In area MSTd neuronal recalibration occurs in accordance with perceptual recalibration, both for vestibular and visual cues.
source: Therefore, in area MSTd neuronal recalibration occurs in accordance with perceptual recalibration, both for vestibular and visual cues.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the MSTd data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In PIVC, the example vestibular neurometric curve shifted to the right, which was consistent with the vestibular perceptual shift.
source: The example vestibular neurometric curve (Figure 4A, top right) shifted to the right, which was consistent with the vestibular perceptual shift (Figure 4A, top left).
evidence: This claim is supported by the example shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Across the population of PIVC neurons, a significant positive correlation was seen between the neuronal and perceptual shifts for the vestibular cue (r = 0.80, p = 9.7 × 10−6, N = 30, Pearson correlation, data pooled across monkeys).
source: Across the population of PIVC neurons, a significant positive correlation was seen between the neuronal and perceptual shifts for the vestibular cue (r = 0.80, p = 9.7 × 10−6, N = 30, Pearson correlation, data pooled across monkeys; Figure 4B, left panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: PIVC neurons did not demonstrate robust responses to the visual stimuli.
source: In general, the PIVC neurons did not demonstrate robust responses to the visual stimuli.
evidence: This is a general observation about PIVC neurons.

claim: The correlation between the neuronal and perceptual shifts for the visual cue in PIVC was not significant (r = 0.26, p = 0.47, N = 10, Pearson correlation, data pooled across monkeys).
source: The correlation between the neuronal and perceptual shifts (performed for those neurons that did pass screening) was not significant for the visual cue (r = 0.26, p = 0.47, N = 10, Pearson correlation, data pooled across monkeys).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A Bayesian Pearson correlation (BF10 = 0.49) supported neither the alternative hypothesis (H1) of a correlation between neuronal and perceptual shifts for the visual cue in PIVC, nor the null hypothesis (H0).
source: A Bayesian Pearson correlation (BF10 = 0.49) supported neither the alternative hypothesis (H1) of a correlation between neuronal and perceptual shifts for the visual cue, nor the null hypothesis (H0).
evidence: This is a statistical result regarding visual recalibration in PIVC.

claim: The lack of support for or against visual recalibration in PIVC primarily reflects the lack of robust tuning to visual heading stimuli in PIVC.
source: The lack of support for or against visual recalibration in PIVC primarily reflects the lack of robust tuning to visual heading stimuli in PIVC.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the PIVC visual results.

claim: In an example VIP neuron, the vestibular neurometric curve shifted rightward, in accordance with the vestibular perceptual shift.

source: The most surprising and intriguing finding in this study was the contrary recalibration of visual tuning in VIP.

source: This study exposed modality-specific recalibration of neuronal signals, resulting from a cross-modal (visual–vestibular) cue conflict.

claim: The results provide novel insights into adult multisensory plasticity, and deepen our understanding regarding the different functions of these multisensory cortical areas.
source: The results therefore provide novel insights into adult multisensory plasticity, and deepen our understanding regarding the different functions of these multisensory cortical areas.

claim: Three male rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta, monkeys D, B, and K) weighing 8–10 kg participated in the experiment.
source: Three male rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta, monkeys D, B, and K) weighing 8–10 kg participated in the experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: All animal surgeries and experimental procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at East China Normal University (IACUC protocol number: Mo20200101).
source: All animal surgeries and experimental procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at East China Normal University (IACUC protocol number: Mo20200101).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: The monkeys were head-fixed and seated in a primate chair which was secured to a six degrees of freedom motion platform during the experiments.
source: During the experiments, the monkeys were head-fixed and seated in a primate chair which was secured to a six degrees of freedom motion platform (Moog, East Aurora, NY, USA; MB-E-6DOF/12/1000 kg).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claim: Vestibular stimuli corresponded to linear movements of the platform.
source: Vestibular stimuli corresponded to linear movements of the platform (for details, see Chen et al., 2013a; Gu et al., 2006; Zhao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a description of the vestibular stimuli, with citations to Chen et al., 2013a; Gu et al., 2006; Zhao et al., 2021.

claim: Visual stimuli were presented on a large computer screen attached to the field coil frame.
source: Visual stimuli were presented on a large computer screen (Philips BDL4225E, Royal Philips, Amsterdam, Netherlands), attached to the field coil frame.
evidence: This is a description of the visual stimuli presentation.

claim: Visual stimuli were programmed in OpenGL to simulate self-motion through a 3D cloud of 'stars'.
source: Visual stimuli were programmed in OpenGL to simulate self-motion through a 3D cloud of 'stars' that occupied a virtual cube space 80 cm wide, 80 cm tall, and 80 cm deep, centered on the central fixation point on the screen.
evidence: This is a description of the visual stimuli.

claim: The self-motion stimulus followed a Gaussian velocity profile with a duration of 1 s, and a displacement amplitude of 13 cm.
source: Each motion stimulus followed a Gaussian velocity profile with a duration of 1 s, and a displacement amplitude of 13 cm (bottom row, Figure 6).
evidence: This is a description of the motion stimulus parameters.

claim: The peak velocity was 0.41 m/s, and the peak acceleration was 2.0 m/s2.
source: The peak velocity was 0.41 m/s, and the peak acceleration was 2.0 m/s2.
evidence: This is a description of the motion stimulus parameters.

claim: The monkeys were trained to report their perceived direction of self-motion in a two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) heading discrimination task.
source: The monkeys were trained to report their perceived direction of self-motion in a two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) heading discrimination task (for details, see Chen et al., 2013a; Gu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a description of the behavioral task, with citations to Chen et al., 2013a; Gu et al., 2008.

claim: In each trial, the monkey primarily experienced a forward motion with a small leftward or rightward component.
source: In each trial, the monkey primarily experienced a forward motion with a small leftward or rightward component.
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus in each trial.

claim: During stimulation, the monkey was required to maintain fixation on a central point, within a 3° × 3° window.
source: During stimulation, the monkey was required to maintain fixation on a central point, within a 3° × 3° window.
evidence: This is a description of the task requirements.

claim: At the end of the trial, the monkeys needed to make a saccade to one of two targets to report their motion percept as leftward or rightward relative to straight ahead.
source: At the end of the trial (after a 300-ms delay period beyond the end of the stimulus), the monkeys needed to make a saccade to one of two targets (located 5° to the left and right of the central fixation point) to report their motion percept as leftward or rightward relative to straight ahead.
evidence: This is a description of the task requirements.

claim: Correct responses were rewarded with a drop of liquid.
source: Correct responses were rewarded with a drop of liquid.
evidence: This is a description of the reward structure.

claim: An unsupervised cue-conflict recalibration protocol previously tested behaviorally in humans and monkeys was used to elicit recalibration.
source: To elicit recalibration, we used an unsupervised cue-conflict recalibration protocol previously tested behaviorally in humans and monkeys (Zaidel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a description of the recalibration protocol, with a citation to Zaidel et al., 2011.

claim: In the pre-recalibration block, only a single-cue (vestibular-only or visual-only) stimulus was presented.
source: This block was used to deduce the baseline performance (psychometric curve) of each modality for the monkeys, thus only a single-cue (vestibular-only or visual-only) stimulus was presented (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the pre-recalibration block.

claim: Ten logarithmically spaced heading angles were tested for each monkey (±16°, ±8°, ±4°, ±2°, and ±1°).
source: Ten logarithmically spaced heading angles were tested for each monkey (±16°, ±8°, ±4°, ±2°, and ±1°).
evidence: This is a description of the heading angles tested.

claim: In the pre-recalibration block, monkeys were rewarded with 95% probability for correct choices, and not rewarded for incorrect choices.
source: To accustom the monkeys to not getting a reward for all the trials, they were rewarded with 95% probability for correct choices, and not rewarded for incorrect choices.
evidence: This is a description of the reward structure in the pre-recalibration block.

claim: In the recalibration block, only combined vestibular–visual cues were presented.
source: Only combined vestibular–visual cues were presented in this block (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a description of the recalibration block.

claim: A discrepancy (Δ) between the vestibular and visual cues was introduced gradually from 2° to 10° (or −2° to −10°) with steps of 2°, and then held at ±10° for the rest of the block.
source: A discrepancy (Δ) between the vestibular and visual cues was introduced gradually from 2° to 10° (or −2° to −10°) with steps of 2°, and then held at ±10° for the rest of the block.
evidence: This is a description of the recalibration block procedure.

claim: This gradual introduction was applied to avoid the monkeys from noticing the discrepancy.
source: This gradual introduction was applied to avoid the monkeys from noticing the discrepancy.
evidence: This is an explanation of the rationale for the gradual introduction of the discrepancy.

claim: In the recalibration block, monkeys only needed to maintain fixation on the central fixation point during the stimulus presentation and did not need to make choices at the end of trials.
source: Unlike the pre-recalibration block, monkeys only needed to maintain fixation on the central fixation point during the stimulus presentation and did not need to make choices at the end of trials.
evidence: This is a description of the task requirements in the recalibration block.

claim: In the recalibration block, monkeys were rewarded for all the trials for which they maintained fixation.
source: They were rewarded for all the trials for which they maintained fixation.
evidence: This is a description of the reward structure in the recalibration block.

claim: In the post-recalibration block, performance for the individual (visual/vestibular) modalities was once again tested using single-cue trials.
source: During this block, performance for the individual (visual/vestibular) modalities was once again tested using single-cue trials (as in the pre-recalibration block).
evidence: This is a description of the post-recalibration block.

claim: Responses to single-cue trials in the post-recalibration block were used to measure recalibration.
source: Responses to these trials were used to measure recalibration.
evidence: This is a description of the purpose of the post-recalibration block.

claim: The single-cue trials in the post-recalibration block were interleaved with combined-cue trials.
source: The single-cue trials were interleaved with combined-cue trials (with a ±10° discrepancy, like the end of the recalibration block, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a description of the post-recalibration block procedure.

claim: The combined-cue trials were interleaved to maintain recalibration while it was measured.
source: The combined-cue trials were interleaved to maintain recalibration while it was measured (for details, see Zaidel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an explanation of the rationale for interleaving combined-cue trials, with a citation to Zaidel et al., 2011.

claim: Extracellular activity was recorded from isolated single neurons in areas MSTd, PIVC, and VIP using tungsten microelectrodes.
source: We recorded extracellular activity from isolated single neurons in areas MSTd, PIVC, and VIP using tungsten microelectrodes (Frederick Haer Company, Bowdoin, ME, USA; tip diameter ~3 μm; impedance, 1–2 MΩ at 1 kHz).
evidence: This is a description of the recording methods.

claim: The target areas (MSTd, PIVC, and VIP) were identified based on the patterns of gray and white matter transitions, magnetic resonance imaging scans, stereotaxic coordinates, and physiological response properties as described previously.
source: The target areas (MSTd, PIVC, and VIP) were identified based on the patterns of gray and white matter transitions, magnetic resonance imaging scans, stereotaxic coordinates, and physiological response properties as described previously (MSTd: Gu et al., 2006; PIVC: Chen et al., 2010; VIP: Chen et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is a description of the methods for identifying the target areas, with citations to Gu et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2011a.

claim: Psychometric plots were constructed by fitting the proportion of 'rightward' choices as a function of heading angle with a cumulative Gaussian distribution function, using the psignifit toolbox for MATLAB.
source: Psychometric plots were constructed by fitting the proportion of 'rightward' choices as a function of heading angle with a cumulative Gaussian distribution function, using the psignifit toolbox for MATLAB (version 2.5.6).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

claim: The psychophysical threshold and PSE were defined, respectively, by the standard deviation (SD, σ) and mean (μ) of the fitted Gaussian function.
source: The psychophysical threshold and PSE were defined, respectively, by the standard deviation (SD, σ) and mean (μ) of the fitted Gaussian function.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

claim: The PSE represents the heading angle that would be perceived as straight ahead, also known as the 'bias'.
source: The PSE represents the heading angle that would be perceived as straight ahead, also known as the 'bias'.
evidence: This is a definition of the PSE.

claim: Neuronal tuning curves were constructed for vestibular and visual cues, pre- and post-recalibration, by calculating the average (baseline subtracted) FR responses, as a function of heading.
source: Neuronal tuning curves were constructed for vestibular and visual cues, pre- and post-recalibration, by calculating the average (baseline subtracted) FR responses, as a function of heading.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

claim: A neuron was considered 'tuned' if the linear regression of FR responses by heading (over the narrow range of stimuli presented: −16° to 16°) had a significant slope (p < 0.05).
source: A neuron was considered 'tuned' if the linear regression of FR responses by heading (over the narrow range of stimuli presented: −16° to 16°) had a significant slope (p < 0.05).
evidence: This is a description of the criterion for considering a neuron 'tuned'.

claim: This selection criterion was selective for neurons that have sloped tuning around straight ahead, and excluded neurons with flat tuning, or a tuning preference, straight ahead.
source: This selection criterion was selective for neurons that have sloped tuning around straight ahead, and excluded neurons with flat tuning, or a tuning preference, straight ahead.
evidence: This is an explanation of the rationale for the selection criterion.

claim: In the cortical areas of interest in this study, a disproportionately large number of neurons have steep tuning slopes around straight ahead.
source: In the cortical areas of interest in this study, a disproportionately large number of neurons have steep tuning slopes around straight ahead (Chen et al., 2011b; Gu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2011b; Gu et al., 2010.

claim: Neurons with steep tuning slopes around straight ahead are most informative for heading discrimination (large Fisher information).
source: These neurons are most informative for heading discrimination (large Fisher information, Gu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gu et al., 2010.

claim: Neurons with relatively flat tuning around straight ahead are less informative for heading discrimination (low Fisher information).
source: By contrast, neurons with relatively flat tuning around straight ahead are less informative for heading discrimination (low Fisher information).
evidence: This is a statement about the informativeness of neurons with flat tuning.

claim: Small shifts can be readily detected in neurons with sloped tuning (but not in those with flat tuning) around straight ahead.
source: Accordingly, small shifts can be readily detected in neurons with sloped tuning (but not in those with flat tuning) around straight ahead.
evidence: This is an explanation of the rationale for focusing on neurons with sloped tuning.

claim: In this study, the focus was on the prevalent neurons with sloped tuning around straight ahead.
source: Therefore, in this study we focused on the prevalent neurons with sloped tuning around straight ahead.
evidence: This is a description of the focus of the study.

claim: For each neuron recorded, neurometric curves (per cue and block) were constructed from the FRs.
source: For each neuron recorded, neurometric curves (per cue and block) were constructed from the FRs (Chen et al., 2013a; Fetsch et al., 2011; Gu et al., 2008; Gu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods, with citations to Chen et al., 2013a; Fetsch et al., 2011; Gu et al., 2008; Gu et al., 2007.

claim: The FRs were first normalized (z-scored) by subtracting the pre-recalibration mean, and dividing by the pre-recalibration SD.
source: For this, the FRs were first normalized (z-scored) by subtracting the pre-recalibration mean, and dividing by the pre-recalibration SD.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

claim: The same (pre-recalibration) mean and SD values were used to normalize both the pre- and post-recalibration FRs (per cue).
source: The same (pre-recalibration) mean and SD values were used to normalize both the pre- and post-recalibration FRs (per cue).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

source: A common reference (pre-recalibration mean, corresponding to z-score = 0) was needed to expose PSE shifts (calculating neurometric curves by comparing responses to positive vs. corresponding negative headings assumes PSE = 0°).
evidence: This is an explanation of the rationale for using a common reference.

claim: For each heading, an ROC (receiver operating characteristic) curve was computed by moving a 'criterion' value from the minimum to the maximum z-score (in 100 steps), and plotting the probability that the z-scores exceeded the criterion vs. whether z-score = 0 (the pre-recalibration mean) exceeded that same criterion, or not (1 or 0, respectively).
source: Then, for each heading, an ROC (receiver operating characteristic) curve was computed by moving a 'criterion' value from the minimum to the maximum z-score (in 100 steps), and plotting the probability that the z-scores exceeded the criterion vs. whether z-score = 0 (the pre-recalibration mean) exceeded that same criterion, or not (1 or 0, respectively).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

claim: The area under the ROC curve reflects the probability that an ideal observer would discriminate the neuronal responses for the given heading to the neuron's preferred (vs. non-preferred) side (right/left), in relation to the pre-recalibration mean.
source: The area under the ROC curve reflects the probability that an ideal observer would discriminate the neuronal responses for the given heading to the neuron's preferred (vs. non-preferred) side (right/left), in relation to the pre-recalibration mean.

claim: For subsequent analyses, only neurons that passed both screening criteria (significant tuning and reliable neurometric PSEs) were included.
source: For subsequent analyses, that is, calculating neurometric shifts (and comparison thereof to perceptual shifts) only neurons that passed both of the following two screening criteria (per cue) were included: (1) significant tuning to the corresponding cue (either pre- or post-recalibration; see Data analysis subsection above for details). (2) Both the pre- and post-recalibration neurometrics produced reliable PSEs (bootstrapped SD of the PSE <10°, both pre- and post-recalibration).
evidence: This is a description of the screening criteria for subsequent analyses.

claim: Neuronal shifts were measured by the difference between the post- and pre-recalibration neurometric PSEs.
source: Neuronal shifts were measured by the difference between the post- and pre-recalibration neurometric PSEs (similar to perceptual shifts, see Equation. 1).
evidence: This is a description of the method for measuring neuronal shifts.

source: For each recording area (MSTd, PIVC, and VIP) and cue (vestibular and visual) neuronal shifts were compared to perceptual shifts, using Pearson correlations (pooling data across monkeys).
evidence: This is a description of the statistical analysis methods.

source: Additionally, to assess the relationship between neuronal and perceptual shifts, while taking into account the differences of individual monkeys, we used an LMM, which allowed for random effects in slope and intercept for the different monkeys.

source: To measure neuronal shifts at different time points during the stimulus, we calculated neurometric shifts based on FRs in narrow (200 ms) windows, in increments of 100 ms.

source: To disassociate the unique contributions of heading stimuli and choices to the neural responses (FRs) we computed Pearson partial correlations between these variables (for details, see Chen et al., 2021; Zaidel et al., 2017).

source: To evaluate differences in monkey behavior (PSE), heading, or choice partial correlations, between pre- and post-recalibration, we used two-tailed paired t-tests.

source: Possible differences in spontaneous (baseline) FRs between pre- and post-recalibration were evaluated using Bayesian paired-samples t-tests (BF10 values).

source: Relationships between neuronal and perceptual shifts were tested using Pearson's correlation coefficients and LMMs.
